course.title: Data Visualization
course.description: Turn numbers into pictures people can trust and act on. You will learn how the eye reads visual encodings, how to pick a chart that fits the question, how color and axes can clarify or mislead, and how to show distributions, relationships, time, and parts of a whole, ending with an honest chart of your own. Structure adapted from open data-visualization curricula on OER Commons (CC BY 4.0); all explanations original.

questions.prompt: Which visual channel does the human eye judge most accurately for comparing quantities?
questions.explanation: Position along a shared scale is the most precisely read channel, which is why bar and dot charts beat pie charts for comparison - see 'Why visualize and the encoding channels'.

questions.prompt: You want to compare a single value across twelve categories. The safest default chart is a...
questions.explanation: A bar chart maps each category to a length on a common axis, which the eye compares easily - see 'Choosing the right chart'.

questions.prompt: A bar chart whose vertical axis starts at 40 instead of 0 tends to...
questions.explanation: Truncating the baseline stretches small gaps into large-looking ones, a classic misleading move - see 'Avoiding chartjunk and misleading axes'.

questions.prompt: To show how a single numeric variable is spread out, you would reach for a...
questions.explanation: A histogram buckets values into bins and shows the shape of the distribution - see 'Showing distributions'.

questions.prompt: The best chart for showing whether two numeric variables move together is a...
questions.explanation: A scatter plot places each observation by its two values, revealing correlation and outliers - see 'Relationships and scatter plots'.

questions.prompt: Roughly what fraction of people have some form of red-green color vision deficiency?
questions.explanation: Around 8 percent of men, near 1 in 12, cannot reliably tell red from green, so color alone is a fragile signal - see 'Color and accessibility'.

questions.prompt: A pie chart works acceptably only when it shows...
options: a few parts of one whole that sum to 100 percent
questions.explanation: Pie charts read angle and area poorly, so they are tolerable only for a handful of parts of a single whole - see 'Part-to-whole comparisons'.

questions.prompt: The main risk of a busy dashboard is that it...
options: buries the key number under decoration and clutter
questions.explanation: Without a clear hierarchy, a dashboard hides the decision-driving metric among noise - see 'Designing dashboards'.

lessons.title: Why visualize and the encoding channels
lessons.grammar_note: An encoding is a rule that maps a data value to a visual property (a number to a bar length, a category to a color); the whole craft is choosing encodings the eye reads well.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain why a chart can beat a table, and rank the common visual channels by how accurately people read them. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, which single channel does the eye judge most precisely when comparing amounts?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A visualization maps data to visual properties called channels: position, length, angle, area, color hue, and color intensity. People do not read all channels equally well. Decades of perception studies rank them from most to least accurate roughly like this: position along a common scale, then length, then angle and slope, then area, then color intensity, and finally color hue. The practical rule follows directly: encode the value you most want your reader to compare using the most accurate channel available, which is almost always position or length. Save weaker channels like hue for categories, not for quantities you need read precisely. A chart beats a table when the question is about comparison, trend, or shape; a table wins when the reader needs exact lookup of individual numbers.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Sales for five regions: a bar chart encodes each value as length on a shared axis, so the ranking is instantly clear - a strong encoding. The same five numbers in a pie chart force the eye to compare angles and areas, both weak channels, so close values look tied. Encoding temperature as the height of a line uses position and works well; encoding it only as a shade from pale to deep red uses color intensity and is far harder to read exactly. If you must show a third variable on a scatter plot, map it to color or size, the weaker channels, and keep the two main variables on the two position axes.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Rank these three channels from most to least accurately read: area, position on a common axis, color hue. 2) You need readers to compare exact revenue across eight products. Bar chart or pie chart? 3) True or false: color hue is a good channel for encoding a precise quantity. 4) A reader needs to look up one country's exact population to the person. Chart or table? 5) On a scatter plot of height versus weight, where should a third variable like age go? Answers: 1) position, then area, then color hue. 2) bar chart, because length on a common axis is read precisely. 3) False - hue is best for categories, not precise amounts. 4) table, for exact lookup. 5) onto a weaker channel such as color or point size, leaving the two axes for height and weight.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: encoding an important quantity as area or hue and expecting precise comparison. Mistake: building a chart when the reader actually needs an exact number, where a table would serve better. Exit: (a) Which channel is read most accurately, position or color hue? (b) Name one task where a table beats a chart. Answers: position along a common scale; exact lookup of an individual value.

lessons.title: Choosing the right chart
lessons.grammar_note: Pick the chart from the question, not the data type alone: comparison, distribution, relationship, composition, and trend each point to a different family of charts.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Match a question to a chart family and defend the choice. Warm-up: you want to compare one value across twelve categories - what is your safe default chart?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Start from the question, not the spreadsheet. Five question types cover most needs. Comparison across categories points to bar charts. Trend over time points to line charts. Relationship between two numbers points to scatter plots. Distribution of one number points to histograms or box plots. Composition, or parts of a whole, points to stacked bars or, sparingly, a pie. Once the family is fixed, small choices follow: sort bars by value when categories have no natural order, use horizontal bars when labels are long, and avoid a second axis unless the two series truly share meaning. The chart that needs the least explanation is usually the right one.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Question: which of eight teams closed the most deals? That is a comparison, so a horizontal bar chart sorted by value answers it at a glance. Question: how did monthly signups change over two years? That is a trend, so a single line chart with time on the horizontal axis fits. Question: do taller people weigh more? That is a relationship, so a scatter plot. Question: how are order values spread out? That is a distribution, so a histogram. Question: what share of revenue comes from each of three product lines? That is composition, so a stacked bar or a small pie. Notice how naming the question all but names the chart.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) You want to show how website traffic changed each week for a year. Which chart? 2) You want to compare average salary across six departments. Which chart? 3) You want to see whether ad spend and sales move together. Which chart? 4) You want the shape of how long support calls last. Which chart? 5) Categories have no natural order in a bar chart - how should you order the bars? Answers: 1) a line chart, time on the horizontal axis. 2) a bar chart, one bar per department. 3) a scatter plot of spend versus sales. 4) a histogram of call durations. 5) sort them by value, largest to smallest, so ranking is easy to read.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: choosing a chart by habit rather than by the question, such as forcing a pie onto a comparison. Mistake: leaving unordered categorical bars in random order, hiding the ranking. Exit: (a) A trend-over-time question calls for which chart family? (b) When categories have no natural order, how do you sort the bars? Answers: a line chart; by value.

lessons.title: The grammar of graphics
lessons.grammar_note: In the grammar of graphics a chart is built in layers: data, a mapping from variables to aesthetics, a geometric mark, a scale, and coordinates - change one layer and you get a new chart from the same data.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe any chart as a stack of layers, and swap one layer to redesign it deliberately. Warm-up: name two different geometric marks that could show the same monthly sales numbers.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The grammar of graphics treats a chart as a recipe with named parts rather than a fixed picture. The data layer is your table of rows and columns. The aesthetic mapping says which column drives which visual property: this column to the x position, that column to the y position, another to color. The geometry, or mark, is the shape drawn for each row: a bar, a point, a line, an area. The scale turns data units into pixels and gives you axes and legends; a scale can be linear or logarithmic. The coordinate system is usually Cartesian but could be polar, which is exactly what turns a stacked bar into a pie. Because the parts are independent, you redesign a chart by changing one layer at a time instead of starting over.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Same data, different mark: monthly revenue mapped with x to month and y to revenue becomes a bar chart with a bar mark, or a line chart with a line mark - only the geometry layer changed. Same data, different scale: plotting values that span 1 to 1,000,000 on a linear y scale crushes the small values, while switching only the scale layer to logarithmic spreads them out. Same data, different coordinates: a single stacked bar of market share drawn in polar coordinates becomes a pie chart - only the coordinate layer changed. Adding a category-to-color mapping splits one line into one line per group without touching the other layers.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the five layers of the grammar of graphics. 2) You have a bar chart and want a line chart of the same numbers - which single layer do you change? 3) Your y values span six orders of magnitude and small ones vanish - which layer do you adjust, and to what? 4) Which layer, changed to polar, turns a stacked bar into a pie? 5) How do you show a separate line per region without changing your data table? Answers: 1) data, aesthetic mapping, geometry (mark), scale, coordinate system. 2) the geometry layer, from bar to line. 3) the scale layer, from linear to logarithmic. 4) the coordinate system layer. 5) add a mapping from the region column to the color aesthetic.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking each chart type is a separate unrelated object rather than a set of layer choices. Mistake: rebuilding from scratch when changing one layer would do. Exit: (a) Which layer decides whether rows are drawn as bars or points? (b) Changing the coordinate system from Cartesian to polar turns a stacked bar into what? Answers: the geometry or mark layer; a pie chart.

questions.prompt: Which visual channel is read most accurately for comparing quantities?
questions.explanation: Position on a shared scale tops the accuracy ranking of channels.

questions.prompt: A question about how a value compares across many categories points to which chart family?
questions.explanation: Comparison across categories is the home ground of the bar chart.

questions.prompt: In the grammar of graphics, the layer that decides whether a row is drawn as a bar or a point is the...
questions.explanation: The geometry (mark) layer sets the shape drawn for each row.

questions.prompt: To spread out y values that span many orders of magnitude, you change which layer, and to what?
questions.explanation: A logarithmic scale layer keeps small and large values both visible.

questions.prompt: A trend-over-time question is best answered by a...
questions.explanation: Time on the horizontal axis with a line mark shows trend clearly.

questions.prompt: Changing only the coordinate system from Cartesian to polar turns a stacked bar into a...
questions.explanation: Polar coordinates wrap the stacked bar into a pie.

lessons.title: Color and accessibility
lessons.grammar_note: Use color to mean one thing at a time: a categorical palette for distinct groups, a sequential palette for ordered magnitude, and a diverging palette for values above and below a midpoint.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Choose the right palette type for your data and make charts readable for color-blind viewers. Warm-up: roughly what fraction of men cannot reliably tell red from green?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Color carries meaning only if the palette matches the data. A categorical palette uses distinct hues for unordered groups like countries or product lines, and should stay under about seven colors before groups blur together. A sequential palette runs light to dark in a single hue for ordered magnitude, such as low to high density. A diverging palette uses two contrasting hues meeting at a neutral midpoint, for data that is meaningfully above or below a center like profit versus loss. Accessibility is not optional: about 1 in 12 men has red-green color vision deficiency, so never rely on color alone. Add a second cue - direct labels, shapes, or position - and prefer color-blind-safe palettes. A quick test is to view the chart in grayscale; if categories still separate, it is robust.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Mapping five unrelated teams: a categorical palette of five distinct, evenly spaced hues, with each series also labeled directly so color is a bonus, not the only signal. Mapping population density from low to high: a single-hue sequential palette from pale to deep blue, since the data is ordered. Mapping temperature anomaly, which can be below or above normal: a diverging palette, cool blue for below, warm red for above, white at zero. A red-and-green pass-fail chart fails for color-blind readers; fixing it means adding a check and cross shape or the words pass and fail, so meaning survives in grayscale.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) You are coloring six unordered product categories - which palette type? 2) You are shading a map by income from low to high - which palette type? 3) You are showing budget variance from a target, both over and under - which palette type? 4) Name one way besides color to distinguish two lines on a chart. 5) What quick test shows whether your chart survives color blindness? Answers: 1) a categorical palette. 2) a sequential palette. 3) a diverging palette. 4) direct labels, different dash patterns, or different marker shapes. 5) view it in grayscale and check the groups still separate.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using a rainbow of many hues for ordered data, which hides the order. Mistake: relying on red versus green as the only signal, invisible to many readers. Exit: (a) Which palette type fits ordered magnitude from low to high? (b) Name one non-color cue you can add for accessibility. Answers: a sequential palette; a direct label, a shape, or a dash pattern.

lessons.title: Avoiding chartjunk and misleading axes
lessons.grammar_note: Chartjunk is any ink that does not carry information; the data-ink ratio is the share of ink that does, and good charts push it high.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Strip decoration that adds no information and spot axis tricks that distort the story. Warm-up: what happens to the apparent gaps between bars when the vertical axis starts at 40 instead of 0?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Chartjunk is ink spent on decoration rather than data: heavy gridlines, three-dimensional effects, drop shadows, background images, and needless legends. The data-ink ratio measures the fraction of ink that actually encodes numbers, and raising it - by deleting clutter - usually makes a chart clearer. Axes are where honest charts are most often broken. For bar charts the value axis must start at zero, because a bar's meaning is its length; a truncated baseline exaggerates small differences. Line charts, which encode change rather than magnitude, may use a non-zero baseline but should label it clearly. Other distortions include inconsistent intervals, dual axes chosen to force a false correlation, and reversed scales. The fix is a habit: label axes, show the baseline, keep intervals even, and delete anything that is not data.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A revenue bar chart with a y axis from 40 to 50 makes a 2 percent rise look enormous; redrawing it from 0 shrinks the bars to their honest proportions. A three-dimensional pie with a tilt makes front slices look bigger than back slices of equal value; a flat chart removes the illusion. A dual-axis chart overlaying ice cream sales and drownings on separately scaled axes suggests one causes the other; separating them or using one honest scale breaks the false impression. A cluttered chart with dark gridlines, a boxed legend, and a textured background becomes clearer when you fade the grid, label lines directly, and drop the texture - same data, more of it visible.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) A bar chart's value axis should start at what number, and why? 2) Give two examples of chartjunk. 3) What does a high data-ink ratio mean? 4) May a line chart use a non-zero baseline? 5) Two unrelated series rise together on a dual-axis chart with different scales - what is the danger? Answers: 1) at zero, because a bar encodes magnitude by length and truncating it exaggerates differences. 2) any two of: three-dimensional effects, heavy gridlines, drop shadows, background images, needless legends. 3) most of the ink is carrying data, not decoration. 4) yes, since it encodes change, but the baseline must be labeled. 5) the mismatched scales can suggest a correlation or causation that is not real.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: truncating a bar chart baseline and calling a tiny change dramatic. Mistake: adding three-dimensional flourishes that distort area and hide data. Exit: (a) Where must a bar chart's value axis begin? (b) Define chartjunk in one phrase. Answers: at zero; ink that decorates but carries no information.

lessons.title: Showing distributions
lessons.grammar_note: A distribution describes how one variable's values are spread; summarize it with center (mean, median), spread (range, standard deviation), and shape (skew, peaks).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Read and build histograms and box plots, and describe a distribution's center, spread, and shape. Warm-up: which single chart shows how one numeric variable is spread out?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A histogram slices a numeric variable into equal bins and draws a bar for how many values fall in each, revealing the shape: symmetric, skewed to one side, or with two peaks. Bin width matters - too wide hides structure, too narrow adds noise. A box plot summarizes the same variable with five numbers: minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile, and maximum, with the box spanning the middle half of the data and points beyond the whiskers flagged as outliers. Box plots shine when comparing a distribution across several groups side by side. Watch the difference between mean and median: in a skewed distribution the mean is pulled toward the long tail while the median stays near the bulk of the data, which is why median income is often reported instead of mean income.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Order values from an online store: a histogram shows most orders are small with a long right tail of a few large orders, a right-skewed shape, so the mean order value sits above the median. A box plot of the same orders puts the median line low in the box with a long upper whisker and several high outliers. Comparing test scores across four classes: four box plots side by side reveal which class has the highest median and which has the widest spread at a glance. A histogram of adult heights is roughly symmetric and bell-shaped, so here mean and median nearly coincide.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which chart shows the shape of a single numeric variable's spread? 2) What five numbers define a box plot? 3) In a right-skewed distribution, is the mean above or below the median? 4) What does a point beyond the whiskers of a box plot indicate? 5) When comparing one numeric variable across six groups, which chart is compact and clear? Answers: 1) a histogram. 2) minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile, maximum. 3) above the median, pulled toward the long right tail. 4) an outlier. 5) side-by-side box plots, one per group.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: choosing a bin width that is far too wide or too narrow, hiding or inventing structure. Mistake: reporting the mean of a skewed distribution as if it were typical, when the median is more representative. Exit: (a) What three aspects summarize any distribution? (b) In a right-skewed distribution, which is larger, mean or median? Answers: center, spread, and shape; the mean.

questions.prompt: A single-hue palette running light to dark is best for...
options: ordered magnitude from low to high
values above and below a midpoint
questions.explanation: A sequential palette encodes ordered magnitude.

questions.prompt: Because about 1 in 12 men has red-green color deficiency, you should...
options: add a second cue besides color
questions.explanation: Never rely on color alone; add labels, shapes, or position.

questions.prompt: A bar chart's value axis must start at zero because a bar encodes value as...
questions.explanation: Truncating the baseline distorts the length that carries the value.

questions.prompt: Which chart reveals the shape of how one numeric variable is spread?
questions.explanation: A histogram bins the values and shows the distribution's shape.

questions.prompt: In a right-skewed distribution, the mean sits...
questions.explanation: The long right tail pulls the mean above the median.

questions.prompt: Ink spent on three-dimensional effects and drop shadows rather than data is called...
questions.explanation: Chartjunk is decoration that carries no information.

lessons.title: Relationships and scatter plots
lessons.grammar_note: Correlation measures how two numeric variables move together, from -1 to +1; correlation is not causation, and a strong pattern may still have a hidden common cause.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Read a scatter plot for direction, strength, and outliers, and resist the leap from correlation to cause. Warm-up: which chart shows whether two numeric variables move together?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A scatter plot places each observation at its pair of values, one variable on each axis. You read three things: direction (do points rise or fall from left to right, a positive or negative relationship), strength (do they hug a line tightly or scatter loosely), and anomalies (outliers sitting far from the crowd). A correlation coefficient near +1 or -1 means a tight linear pattern, near 0 means little linear relationship. Two warnings guard against error. First, correlation is not causation: two variables can move together because a third drives both, or by pure coincidence. Second, a correlation coefficient can miss a strong non-linear pattern, so always look at the plot, not just the number. When points overlap heavily, use transparency or smaller marks so density stays visible.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Height versus weight for adults: points rise from lower left to upper right, a positive relationship of moderate strength, with a couple of outliers who are tall but light. Hours studied versus exam score: a positive trend, tighter than the height example, so the correlation is closer to +1. Ice cream sales versus drownings across the year: strongly correlated, but the hidden common cause is summer heat, not one causing the other - a textbook reminder that correlation is not causation. A U-shaped scatter of stress versus performance has a correlation coefficient near zero even though the relationship is real, because the pattern is non-linear.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) On a scatter plot, what do you call points that rise from left to right? 2) A correlation coefficient of -0.9 means the relationship is what direction and how strong? 3) Ice cream sales and drownings both peak in summer - what explains the correlation? 4) Why can a correlation near 0 still hide a real relationship? 5) Points overlap into a solid blob - name one fix. Answers: 1) a positive relationship. 2) negative and strong. 3) a hidden common cause, summer heat, not causation. 4) the relationship may be non-linear, which the coefficient does not capture. 5) use transparency or smaller markers to reveal density.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading a strong correlation as proof that one variable causes the other. Mistake: trusting the correlation number without looking at the scatter, missing non-linear shapes. Exit: (a) What range does a correlation coefficient span? (b) Name one reason two correlated variables need not have a causal link. Answers: -1 to +1; a hidden common cause or coincidence.

lessons.title: Time series
lessons.grammar_note: A time series is data indexed by time; read it for trend (long-run direction), seasonality (repeating cycles), and noise (short-run wobble).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Build and read line charts over time, separating trend, seasonality, and noise, and smooth a jagged series honestly. Warm-up: which chart family answers a how-did-this-change-over-time question?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Time series data belongs on a line chart with time on the horizontal axis, points in chronological order, and even time intervals so the slope means what it appears to mean. Three components live inside most series. The trend is the long-run direction, up, down, or flat. Seasonality is a repeating pattern tied to the calendar, such as higher retail sales every December. Noise is the short-term random wobble on top. A moving average smooths the noise by averaging each point with its neighbors, making the trend easier to see, but a longer window hides more detail, so state the window you used. Keep the time axis evenly spaced and never reorder points; connecting dots that are not in time order produces a meaningless tangle.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Monthly retail sales over three years: a rising trend, a clear December spike each year (seasonality), and small month-to-month wobble (noise). A 12-month moving average flattens the December spikes and reveals the underlying upward trend. Daily website traffic: very noisy day to day, so a 7-day moving average exposes the weekly pattern and the slow rise. A stock price line with uneven gaps for weekends, drawn as if evenly spaced, misleads about the rate of change; spacing the axis by real dates fixes it. Plotting quarterly revenue but connecting quarters out of order yields a zigzag that means nothing.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) On what axis does time belong in a line chart? 2) Name the three components of a typical time series. 3) What does a moving average do to noise? 4) Why must the time axis use even intervals? 5) A daily series is too jagged to read - what simple tool helps? Answers: 1) the horizontal axis. 2) trend, seasonality, and noise. 3) it smooths or averages the noise out, revealing the trend. 4) so the slope honestly reflects the rate of change. 5) a moving average, for example a 7-day window.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using uneven time spacing so the slope lies about how fast things changed. Mistake: over-smoothing with too long a window until real features vanish, without stating the window. Exit: (a) Repeating calendar patterns in a time series are called what? (b) What does a moving average reveal by reducing noise? Answers: seasonality; the underlying trend.

lessons.title: Part-to-whole comparisons
lessons.grammar_note: Part-to-whole (composition) shows how a total breaks into pieces that sum to 100 percent; the pieces, not just the total, are the point.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Show composition clearly and know when a pie chart is acceptable and when a bar chart wins. Warm-up: under what one condition is a pie chart tolerable?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Composition charts answer what share each part contributes to a whole. The pie chart is the famous choice, but it asks the eye to compare angles and areas, both weak channels, so it works only for a few slices - roughly two to five - of a single whole that sum to 100 percent. Beyond a handful of slices, or when parts are close in size, a bar chart of the same shares is easier to rank and read. To show composition changing over time, a stacked bar or stacked area chart works, but only the bottom band sits on a flat baseline, so upper bands are hard to compare precisely; if one part's trend matters most, give it its own line. A common honest fix is to simply label each slice or bar with its percentage.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Three product lines' share of revenue: a pie with three clearly different slices, each labeled with its percentage, reads fine. Twelve marketing channels' share: a pie becomes a ring of thin, similar slices no one can rank, so a sorted bar chart of the same percentages is far clearer. Budget composition across five years: a stacked bar per year shows the whole growing and the mix shifting, but because upper segments float, if the research-and-development share is the story, a single line for that share alone is more precise. Two nearly equal slices in a pie look identical; a bar chart exposes which is larger.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) A pie chart is acceptable for about how many slices? 2) You have twelve categories of similar size - pie or sorted bar? 3) Why are upper bands of a stacked bar hard to compare? 4) One part's trend over time matters most - what shows it precisely? 5) Name a simple label that makes any composition chart more honest. Answers: 1) about two to five slices of one whole. 2) a sorted bar chart. 3) they do not share a flat baseline, so their lengths start at shifting positions. 4) a single line dedicated to that part's share. 5) the percentage printed on each slice or bar.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: crowding a pie with many thin slices no one can compare. Mistake: expecting precise comparison of the upper bands of a stacked chart, which float off the baseline. Exit: (a) A pie chart works only for parts of a whole that sum to what? (b) For many similar-sized categories, which chart beats a pie? Answers: 100 percent; a sorted bar chart.

lessons.title: Designing dashboards
lessons.grammar_note: A dashboard is a single screen of linked views built around a decision; design it top-down by importance, not by cramming in every metric you have.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Lay out a dashboard with a clear hierarchy so the key metric is found in seconds. Warm-up: what is the main risk of a busy dashboard?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A dashboard collects several charts on one screen to support a specific decision or audience. Its enemy is clutter, so start from one question: what must the viewer decide, and what single number drives it? Place that headline metric top-left, where reading habits land first, and make it large. Supporting charts fan out below and to the right in decreasing importance. Group related views and align them on a grid so the eye moves smoothly. Keep the encodings consistent - the same color should mean the same category in every panel. Prefer a few clear charts over many tiny ones, and add short, plain titles that state the takeaway rather than just the variable. Every element should earn its place by informing the decision; if it does not, remove it.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A sales dashboard for a manager: the headline is this quarter's revenue against target, shown big at top-left; below it, a line of revenue over time, a sorted bar of revenue by region, and a small table of top deals, each titled with its point such as 'Revenue is 8 percent ahead of target.' Colors stay consistent - each region keeps one hue across every panel. A cluttered version with fifteen equal-sized charts, three color schemes, and no clear starting point forces the viewer to hunt; fixing it means cutting to the four charts that drive the decision, unifying the palette, and enlarging the headline number. A support dashboard leads with open tickets and median response time, the two numbers a lead acts on.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Where does the most important metric usually go on a dashboard? 2) What single question should shape the whole layout? 3) Why must a category keep the same color across panels? 4) Better to show four clear charts or fifteen tiny ones? 5) What should a panel title state beyond the variable name? Answers: 1) top-left, large. 2) what decision must the viewer make, and what number drives it. 3) so the same color always means the same thing and the eye is not confused across panels. 4) four clear charts. 5) the takeaway or point of that chart.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: cramming every available metric onto one screen with no hierarchy. Mistake: letting a color mean one category in one panel and a different one elsewhere. Exit: (a) Where does the headline metric belong? (b) What is the single guiding question for a dashboard's layout? Answers: top-left and large; what decision must the viewer make and which number drives it.

questions.prompt: A correlation coefficient near +1 means the two variables have a...
questions.explanation: Values near +1 indicate a tight positive linear pattern.

questions.prompt: Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in summer. The best explanation is...
options: a hidden common cause, summer heat
questions.explanation: A third variable drives both; correlation is not causation.

questions.prompt: Repeating calendar patterns in a time series, like December sales spikes, are called...
questions.explanation: Seasonality is the recurring, calendar-linked component.

questions.prompt: A pie chart is acceptable only when it shows...
options: a few parts of one whole summing to 100 percent
questions.explanation: Pies read angle poorly, so keep to a few parts of a single whole.

questions.prompt: On a dashboard, the single most important metric usually belongs...
questions.explanation: Reading habits land first at top-left, so the headline goes there, large.

questions.prompt: A moving average is used on a time series mainly to...
options: smooth noise and reveal the trend
questions.explanation: Averaging neighbors reduces short-term wobble so the trend shows.

lessons.title: Capstone: build an honest chart
lessons.grammar_note: An honest chart states its question, uses the strongest encoding for the key value, keeps axes and color truthful, and needs little explanation to be understood.

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Take a small dataset you have - or the sample below - and produce one finished, honest chart with a written rationale. Sample data: monthly signups for a year, 120, 135, 150, 148, 170, 210, 205, 230, 260, 255, 300, 340. Your deliverable is the chart plus three or four sentences naming the question it answers, the chart family you chose and why, and the encoding, axis, and color decisions you made.

sections.heading: The structure to follow
sections.text: 1) State the question in one sentence (for the sample: how did signups change over the year?). 2) Choose the chart family from the question type - comparison, trend, relationship, distribution, or composition. 3) Pick the mark and map the key value to the strongest channel, position or length. 4) Make the axes honest: zero baseline for bars, labeled baseline for lines, even intervals on a time axis. 5) Use color with a purpose and add a non-color cue so it survives grayscale. 6) Strip chartjunk and write a title that states the takeaway, not just the variable.

sections.heading: A fully worked model (different data)
sections.text: Question: which of six regions closed the most deals last quarter? This is a comparison, so the family is a bar chart. Mark: horizontal bars, one per region, mapping deals-closed to length on a common axis - the strongest channel. Axis: the value axis starts at zero so bar lengths are truthful; bars are sorted largest to smallest since regions have no natural order. Color: a single neutral hue for all bars, with the leading region highlighted and also labeled with its value, so the emphasis survives in grayscale. Chartjunk: gridlines faded, no three-dimensional effect, legend dropped because bars are labeled directly. Title: 'North closed the most deals, 42, nearly double the South.' Use this as a template of reasoning - do not copy it; your job is the signups question above, which is a trend and therefore calls for a line chart, not bars.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Work the sample before checking. 1) Is the signups question a comparison, trend, or distribution? 2) Which chart family follows? 3) On which axis does the month go? 4) May the line chart use a non-zero baseline, and what must you do if it does? 5) Name one non-color cue to mark the final, highest month. Answers: 1) a trend over time. 2) a line chart. 3) the horizontal axis. 4) yes, since a line encodes change, but the baseline must be clearly labeled. 5) a direct data label on the last point, or a distinct marker shape - either survives grayscale.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: Check yes to each: the chart states its question in a plain-language title; the chart family matches the question type; the key value uses position or length, the strongest channels; the axes are honest, with a zero baseline for bars and a labeled baseline and even intervals for a time axis; color has a clear purpose and a non-color cue backs it up; chartjunk is removed so nearly all ink carries data. If all six are true, you have built an honest chart.

questions.prompt: The most accurately read visual channel for comparing quantities is...
questions.explanation: Position on a shared scale tops the perceptual accuracy ranking - see 'Why visualize and the encoding channels'.

questions.prompt: A question about how one value compares across many categories is best shown with a...
questions.explanation: Comparison across categories calls for a bar chart - see 'Choosing the right chart'.

questions.prompt: In the grammar of graphics, switching only the geometry layer from bar to line changes...
options: the mark drawn for each row
questions.explanation: The geometry (mark) layer sets the shape; the data stays the same - see 'The grammar of graphics'.

questions.prompt: For data that runs from low to high magnitude, the right palette is...
questions.explanation: A sequential single-hue palette encodes ordered magnitude - see 'Color and accessibility'.

questions.prompt: A bar chart's value axis is truncated to start at 40. This mainly...
questions.explanation: Bars encode magnitude by length, so a non-zero baseline distorts them - see 'Avoiding chartjunk and misleading axes'.

questions.prompt: In a right-skewed distribution, the mean sits where relative to the median?
options: above it, pulled by the long tail
questions.explanation: The long right tail pulls the mean above the median - see 'Showing distributions'.

questions.prompt: A strong correlation between two variables proves that...
questions.explanation: Correlation is not causation; a third variable or coincidence may explain it - see 'Relationships and scatter plots'.

questions.prompt: Repeating December spikes in monthly sales are an example of...
questions.explanation: Calendar-linked repeating cycles are seasonality - see 'Time series'.

questions.prompt: For twelve categories of similar size, the clearest composition chart is a...
questions.explanation: Many similar slices defeat a pie; a sorted bar chart ranks them clearly - see 'Part-to-whole comparisons'.

questions.prompt: The most important metric on a dashboard usually belongs...
questions.explanation: Reading order lands first at top-left, so the headline metric goes there, large - see 'Designing dashboards'.
